summary:
Palau decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2014. The Penal Code signed by the President in April 2014 dropped the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment. Palau's Attorney General confirmed the repeal. No offence against consensual same-sex conduct is in force.

Until that repeal the prohibition was live. A 2011 survey of Pacific and global jurisdictions listed Palau among more than 70 jurisdictions whose laws still criminalised same-sex relations.

Palau accepted recommendations to end criminalisation at its 2011 Universal Periodic Review, and at the same review accepted recommendations to combat discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Palau and Nauru both accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council review appearances, which documents a stated commitment to repeal rather than an unprompted legislative initiative.

On 22 March 2011, Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint statement to the Human Rights Council calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That statement is the earliest dated record of Palau's position in the inventory.
tangentialFactors:
The 2014 repeal lowered the global count of countries retaining anti-sodomy provisions to 79, according to the Human Dignity Trust figures cited at the time. Palau's action therefore reads as one of a small number of repeals in that period rather than an isolated event.

Nauru accepted the same decriminalisation recommendation in the same review cycle, so the direction of travel across these two small Pacific states was consistent in 2011.

The sourced record stops in 2014. Nothing in the inventory covers enforcement practice, police conduct, prosecutions, or reported violence against trans people in Palau after that date, so the current social climate cannot be assessed from these sources.
localsOnly:
The repeal was carried out through the consolidated Penal Code rather than a stand-alone amendment, so the operative domestic text for residents is the Penal Code as signed in April 2014, with the former section 2803 of Chapter 28 no longer part of Title 17.

The recommendations Palau accepted at its 2011 Universal Periodic Review are commitments Palau's government made to the international review process, covering both the repeal of criminalisation and measures against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Their implementation beyond the 2014 repeal is not documented in the inventory.

The March 2011 joint statement was delivered to the Human Rights Council on Palau's behalf alongside 83 other countries, and stands as a diplomatic position Palau has publicly associated itself with.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, change of marker on passports or national identification, entry or visa screening that could disclose trans status, restroom or facility access, restrictions on gender-affirming healthcare, hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity, or recognition of partners and marriages. Those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

Whether any residual provision of the 2014 Penal Code, such as a public-morality or conduct offence not framed as sodomy, could still be applied to trans people is not documented in the sources.

No post-2014 reporting on enforcement practice, court decisions, or documented violence against trans people in Palau appears in the inventory, so the practical position after decriminalisation is unverified.
